tabbit.declaration-needs-name: `{Written}` declares a {Kind} and names none. Write the name after the keyword - `:{Kind} Item`.
tabbit.declaration-meta-unclosed: `{Written}` opens a bracket and never closes it. The brackets on a declaration hold its settings - `:table Item(side=s)`.
tabbit.declaration-meta-key-unknown: `{Written}` sets `{Key}`, which a {Kind} declaration does not take. It takes: {Known}.
tabbit.declaration-meta-key-repeated: `{Written}` sets `{Key}` twice. One value, or the second quietly replaces the first.
tabbit.declaration-meta-value-missing: `{Written}` names `{Key}` with no value. Write one - `{Example}`.
tabbit.declaration-meta-key-not-on-kind: `{Written}` sets `{Key}`, and a `:{Kind}` does not take it - {Because}.
tabbit.entity-name-duplicated: `{Name}` is declared twice - as {Kind} here, and already above. A name identifies one entity whatever its kind, because the generated code has one name for it.
tabbit.marker-column-unknown: The marker column of `{Entity}` holds `{Written}`, and this layout defines no row key of that name. It takes a declaration (`:table`, `:enum`, `:const`), a header row key ({Keys}), `#` to leave the row out, a row tag written without the leading colon, or nothing at all for a data row.
tabbit.row-tag-beside-omit-mark: The marker column of `{Entity}` holds `{Written}`, which is neither `#` nor a tag. `#` alone leaves the row out of every build; `{Tag}` on its own is a tag, which leaves it out of the builds whose recipe names it. Written together it would be read as a tag called `{Written}`, and the row would ship.
tabbit.row-key-repeated: `{Entity}` has two `{Key}` rows. Which one is read would then depend on the order they happen to be in.
tabbit.row-key-below-data: `{Entity}` has a `{Key}` row below a data row. Header rows come before the data - a sheet sorted with its header rows in the selection lands here.
tabbit.field-row-missing: `{Entity}` has no `:field` row. It is the one header row that cannot be left out, because nothing else says what the columns are.
tabbit.type-row-missing: Table `{Entity}` has no `:type` row. Every field column states its type.
tabbit.type-row-not-on-entity: `{Entity}` is {Kind} and has a `:type` row. The columns of {Kind} are fixed and named in `:field`, so there is no type for a row to state.
tabbit.row-key-not-on-entity: `{Entity}` is {Kind} and has a `{Key}` row, which {Kind} has no use for. It takes: {Keys}.
tabbit.column-unnamed-with-data: Column {Column} of `{Entity}` has no name in `:field`, and `{Value}` is written below it. Name it if it is a field; write `#` in its `:field` cell if it is space for the sheet's author, which nothing reads.
tabbit.column-type-missing: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` has no type. Write one in its `:type` cell. A blank type cell is how a group's later members and an array's later elements say the first one already stated it - which this column is not.
tabbit.no-field-columns: `{Entity}` has no column carrying a field. Every column is either unnamed or marked `#`.
tabbit.element-number-not-integer: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` is numbered `{Written}`, which is not a whole number.
tabbit.element-numbers-not-from-zero: `{Entity}.{Group}` starts at element {First}. Element numbers count from zero and run without a gap, so the first column of a group is `[0]`.
tabbit.element-numbers-not-consecutive: `{Entity}.{Group}` has element {Present} and not element {Missing}. Element numbers run without a gap - an array cannot be missing its middle.
tabbit.index-mark-on-array-column: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` is marked `*`, and it holds an array. An index addresses one row by one value, which an array is not. If `*` was meant as a multi-row mark, this layout writes that with `[]` on the name and `*` is the secondary index.
tabbit.repeated-index-mark: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` begins with more than one `*`. One marks a secondary index.
tabbit.index-mark-on-group-member: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` is marked `*` and is a member of `{Group}`. An index addresses a row by a field of its own.
tabbit.multi-row-nested: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` writes `[]` beside another repeating level. A `[]` group whose member repeats again would replicate the whole set of columns per element, which this layout does not read. Write the inner array as a delimited cell or as numbered columns.
tabbit.multi-row-cell-array: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` is written `[]` and typed `{Written}`. The name says the elements come from the rows below and the type says they come from inside the cell, so each row would hold an array of them - which this layout does not read. Pick one place for the elements.
tabbit.multi-row-on-index-column: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` is written `[]` and is the column the primary index is read from. An index addresses one row by one value, which an array is not.
tabbit.extension-row-has-scalar-value: `{Value}` is written in column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` on a row that extends the record above it. Only `[]` columns carry values on an extension row - this one belongs on the record's first row. If a new record was meant, write its index.
tabbit.extension-row-without-record: `{Entity}` has a row with no index value before any record has begun. A row that leaves the index blank extends the record above it, and here there is none.
tabbit.variant-duplicated: Field `{Column}` of `{Entity}` has two columns for the variant `{Variant}`. Which one became the field would then depend on the order they happen to be in.
tabbit.variant-not-found: This build asks for the variant `{Variant}` of `{Entity}.{Column}`, and no column of it names one. It has: {Known}.
tabbit.variant-not-chosen: Every column of `{Entity}.{Column}` names a variant, so there is no default for a build to fall back to. Ask for one - `--variant {Entity}.{Column}=…` or the recipe’s `Variants` - from: {Known}.
tabbit.variant-header-disagrees: The variant `{Variant}` of `{Entity}.{Column}` is typed `{Written}`, and the field is typed `{Canonical}`. A field is one field whichever variant a build takes, so its columns state one type - write it once on the default column, or write the same thing.
tabbit.variant-on-key-column: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` carries a variant and is a column the row is addressed by. The identity of a row cannot differ between builds - a reference, a history entry and a deployment comparison would all be about a row nothing else can name.
tabbit.variant-on-group-column: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` carries a variant and is part of a group. A variant of a group would repeat the whole set of columns per variant, which this build does not read - write the variants as separate fields.
tabbit.reserved-column-not-yet-supported: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` ends in `{Name}`, a name this layout reserves. `$type` names the variant of a polymorphic record, `$key` the key of a map and `$value` a variant packed into one cell - each waits on the design that settles what it means, and none of them is read yet. A reserved name is judged at the last step of the path, so `effect.{Name}` is reserved too. Reserved: {Reserved}.
tabbit.column-meta-unclosed: Column `{Column}` of `{Entity}` is typed `{Written}`, which opens a bracket and never closes it. Everything from the first `(` is the column meta - `int (min=0, max=100)`.
tabbit.multi-target-reference-removed: `{Entity}.{Column}` is typed `foreign {Written}`, which names several tables. A reference names one table and resolves it, and a value that may be an id of any of several has no single type to resolve to - so that is a check rather than a reference. Write it as `refs={Refs}` and the column keeps the type it has, or give each table a column of its own.
tabbit.key-column-not-found: `{Entity}` sets `key` to `{Key}`, and no column of it is named that. Its columns are: {Known}.
tabbit.key-column-not-scalar: `{Entity}` sets `key` to `{Key}`, which is part of a group rather than a column of its own. A row is addressed by one value of one of its own columns.
tabbit.key-meta-empty: `{Entity}` sets `key` to `{Written}`, which names no column. A key is one column or several - `key=code`, or `key="stage,slot"`.
tabbit.key-component-repeated: The key `{Key}` of `{Entity}` names `{Column}` twice. A column takes part in a key once; naming it again narrows nothing.
tabbit.key-declared-twice: `{Entity}` declares the key `{Key}` twice. A `*` beside a column and a one-column `key` are the same declaration written two ways, and two keys over the same columns hold the same rows unique.
tabbit.enum-column-unknown: Enum `{Entity}` has a column named `{Column}`, which this layout does not define. It takes: {Known}.
tabbit.enum-column-missing: Enum `{Entity}` has no `{Column}` column, and needs one.
tabbit.enum-label-value-not-integer: Label `{Label}` of enum `{Entity}` has the value `{Value}`, which is not a whole number.
tabbit.enum-cell-required: A label of enum `{Entity}` leaves its `{Column}` cell blank. Both the name and the value of a label are required.
tabbit.enum-alias-duplicated: Enum `{Entity}` has two labels aliased `{Alias}`. An alias is a fourth way to write a label in a data cell, so two labels sharing one would make that cell mean either.
tabbit.enum-alias-shadows-label: Label `{Label}` of enum `{Entity}` is aliased `{Alias}`, which is already the name of the label `{Shadowed}`. A real name always answers a cell first, so this alias resolves nothing - and a cell written with it reaches `{Shadowed}` rather than `{Label}`.
tabbit.constant-column-unknown: Constant set `{Entity}` has a column named `{Column}`, which this layout does not define. It takes: {Known}.
tabbit.constant-column-missing: Constant set `{Entity}` has no `{Column}` column, and needs one.
tabbit.constant-redefined: Constant set `{Entity}` has two constants named `{Name}`.
tabbit.constant-cannot-be-optional: Constant `{Name}` of `{Entity}` is typed `{Type}`. A constant is one value written in one cell - there is no row for it to be absent from, so `?` has nothing to mean here.
tabbit.constant-cell-required: Constant `{Name}` of `{Entity}` leaves its `{Column}` cell blank. The name, the type and the value of a constant are all required.
tabbit.constant-type-not-array-element: Constant `{Entity}.{Name}` is typed as an array of `{Type}`, and `{Type}` is not a type this tool puts in an array. The array types are the scalar ones and an enum - a composite value type, a struct and a reference are not among them.
tabbit.composite-key-multi-row: `{Entity}` is a multi-row table whose primary key `{Key}` is several columns taken together. A multi-row record begins where the primary key's cell has a value, and a combination spread over several columns has no such cell - so where one record ends and the next begins cannot be read. Give the table a single-column primary key, or write one row per record.
tabbit.col-row-missing: `{Entity}` is a grid and has no `:col` row. That row holds the column axis - its name and type in the first cell, its keys across the rest.
tabbit.matrix-needs-two-columns: `{Entity}` is a grid and has only one column. A grid needs the row axis column and at least one grid column beside it.
tabbit.matrix-name-missing: `{Entity}` leaves the {Which} unnamed in its `:field` row. The first cell names the row axis and the second names the grid.
tabbit.matrix-name-marked: `{Written}` in `{Entity}` carries `{Mark}`, which a grid does not take. A grid's columns are keys carried in the data, so there is no wire tag to set, no tombstone to reserve and no second index to mark.
tabbit.matrix-header-beyond-grid: `{Written}` in `{Entity}` sits past the grid's first column. A grid is one group, so it is named and typed once - the columns after it are keys, and the `:col` row is what says so.
tabbit.matrix-column-axis-missing: `{Entity}` leaves the first cell of its `:col` row blank. That cell names the column axis and gives its type - `goods foreign Goods`.
tabbit.matrix-column-axis-needs-type: `{Written}` in `{Entity}` names the column axis and gives no type. Write the type behind the name - `goods foreign Goods`.
tabbit.matrix-no-column-keys: `{Entity}` is a grid whose `:col` row holds no keys. The cells after the first are the column axis keys, and a grid needs at least one.
tabbit.enum-name-already-declared: `{Name}` is declared here and a type of that name is already declared at {Where}. Two enums of one name leave nothing to say which a type cell or a data cell meant; rename one of them, or keep the declaration and delete the sheet's.
